topic: Research: Make vs Zapier vs n8n (2026): Which Automation Tool Wins?

key_points: Positions Zapier as the easiest option with the largest app directory.
Frames Make as the visual-power/value choice for branching workflows.
Frames n8n as the strongest value for self-hosting, high-volume automation, and data control.
Emphasizes n8n cost advantages for complex, high-volume workflows.
Compares the three tools by workflow complexity, cost model, and technical skill required.
Highlights self-hosted n8n as attractive when execution limits or data residency matter.
Compares n8n and Make from Zapier's perspective, with Make described as more plug-and-play and n8n as more build-and-maintain.
Argues Make has more ready integrations while n8n has stronger AI-oriented flexibility.
Stresses operational responsibility: n8n can give more control, but security, hosting, and scaling require more work.
Places n8n, Zapier, Make, and other platforms in a broader 2026 AI workflow automation landscape.
Segments tools by technical skill, business size, and AI automation needs.
Makes AI workflows, agentic automation, and developer flexibility central to the buying decision.
Summarizes the market as Zapier for integrations, Make for visual workflow power, and n8n for fair-code flexibility.
Calls out Zapier's cost at scale, Make's affordability, and n8n's free/self-hosted option.
Useful competitor structure: simple pros/cons and buyer-fit sections rather than a pure feature table.

stats.fact: Zapier advertises automation across 9,000+ apps and says it is trusted by 3 million+ businesses.
Zapier's official pricing page lists Professional from $19.99/month billed annually with a 750-task tier, and Zapier Help describes a Professional 750 plan task limit.
Make advertises 3,000+ pre-built apps, 400+ pre-built AI app integrations, and visual AI/agentic workflow automation.

Make's pricing page lists Free at 1,000 credits/month, Core at $12/month for 10,000 credits/month, Pro at $21/month, and Teams at $38/month on monthly pricing; each module action counts as one credit.
n8n says all cloud plans include unlimited users and workflows plus every integration, with pricing based on monthly workflow executions regardless of complexity.
n8n's pricing page describes Starter trial limits of 2,500 executions, 5 concurrent executions, and 20 AI Workflow Builder credits.
n8n's AI agents page describes agents that make decisions, interact with apps, execute tasks, use tools like web search or databases, and can be self-hosted for data control.
Mordor Intelligence estimates the workflow automation market at $26.01 billion in 2026, growing to $40.77 billion by 2031 at a 9.41% CAGR.
Zapier's 2026 automation statistics article cites World Economic Forum data that 73% of employers intend to accelerate automation of processes and tasks by 2030.

angles: Do not declare one universal winner; make the winner depend on team profile: Zapier for non-technical speed and app coverage, Make for visual operations teams balancing power and cost, n8n for developers, AI-agent builders, privacy-sensitive teams, and high-volume workflows.
The real 2026 comparison is billing model, not just feature lists: Zapier bills tasks, Make bills credits/operations, and n8n bills workflow executions on cloud or infrastructure if self-hosted.
AI changes the category: buyers now need to compare not only triggers and actions, but also agent nodes, MCP/AI actions, AI workflow builders, governance, observability, and human approval paths.
Self-hosting is an advantage only if the team can operate it; n8n's low execution cost can turn into engineering ownership, monitoring, upgrades, and security work.
Make is the middle-ground story: more visual and controllable than Zapier for branching workflows, less infrastructure burden than self-hosted n8n.
Zapier remains strongest when integration breadth, templates, and handoff to non-technical teams matter more than execution-cost optimization.
For developers, the decisive questions are custom code, API/webhook flexibility, version control/deployment workflow, secrets handling, and whether workflows need to become production systems.
